Do the following using the steps provided in their respective sections.
        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis. 
            2.2 kubernetes yamls based on the analysis.
            2.3 github actions file to build application on pushing to main branch.
        3. add all changed file to git changes 
        4. commit / push to repo

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the task.  
I’ll also include the exact files that should end up in the repository so you can verify them before committing.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually run `git clone`, `git push`, etc. from here, but the commands below will do it for you on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you don’t have SSH keys set up, you can use HTTPS instead:
> ```bash
> git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
> cd nodejs-welcome
> ```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

```bash
# Quick look at the tree
tree -L 2
```

Typical output (you may see something like this):

```
nodejs-welcome/
├── src/
│   └── index.js
├── package.json
└── README.md
```

* `src/index.js` – the entry point of the Node.js app  
* `package.json` – contains dependencies and start script

### 2.2 Create a Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install app dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Define the command to run the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> *Why `node:18-alpine`?*  
> Alpine images are small and fast; Node 18 is the LTS version most projects target today.

### 2.3 Create Kubernetes YAML files

Create a directory called `k8s` (or put the files directly in the repo root).  
Inside it, create two files: `deployment.yaml` and `service.yaml`.

#### `deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
```

#### `service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # change to NodePort or ClusterIP if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Tip** – If you’re deploying to a local cluster (e.g., Minikube), you might want to use `NodePort` instead of `LoadBalancer`.

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout source
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      # Uncomment and configure if you want to deploy automatically
      # uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v3
      # with:
      #   manifests: k8s/*.yaml
      #   kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
```

> **What you need to set up:**
> * `DOCKER_USERNAME` and `DOCKER_PASSWORD` secrets in the repo settings (for Docker Hub or any registry you use).
> * Optionally, a `KUBECONFIG` secret if you want the workflow to deploy automatically.

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to Git

```bash
# Stage the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

If you prefer to stage everything at once:

```bash
git add .
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.

---

## 🎉 Verify

After pushing, you should see:

* A new **Actions** tab with a successful run (once you push again).
* The Docker image built and pushed to your registry.
* The Kubernetes manifests available in the repo.

You can now apply the manifests locally or to your cluster:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/
```

---

### Recap of the files added

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deploys 2 replicas of the app |
| `k8s/service.yaml` | Exposes the app via a LoadBalancer |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | Builds & pushes Docker image on every push to `main` |

Feel free to tweak the Docker image tag, registry, or Kubernetes service type to match your environment. Happy coding!
